prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The distinguishing idea is the magic-wavelength lattice: it cancels the light shift of the clock transition, so that very many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without perturbing the transition. That is what turned optical clocks from a single-ion line into a high-stability, high-accuracy neutral-atom line. The outcome is measurable and independently confirmed: uncertainties near 1e-18 in several laboratories, with Sr and Yb in different countries, now beyond the caesium definition. Ye's programme made it a tool for new tests (redshift across millimetre scales, clock comparisons, constraints on variation of constants), so it is already producing physics and not only promising it. The two-name credit is the only one on the shortlist that I can defend without a visible excluded contributor at the core. I do not need the pending redefinition of the second for the argument, and as Lindroth said I would keep it out of the citation. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice, which separates it by wording from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems.
statement.case_against: The risk I take most seriously is the one Mehlig, Eriksson and Danielsson all press: that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already covered the toolbox, so a lattice-clock prize reads as measurement progress in an honoured field and not as a new discovery. I judge the lattice scheme to be a distinct invention, but that is a judgement and I do not claim it settles the point for colleagues whose weighting differs. A second concern is credit: other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, and Derevianko on theory) and the ion-clock groups are outside two names, and I rely on recollection of the priority history, not verified documents. Third, topological insulators carry a conceptual weight that a clock does not, and I accept that if the committee ranks conceptual reclassification above capability, B047 is the stronger prize in principle; its obstacle for me is credit and overlap with 2016, not merit.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio first as a new organising principle and in round 1 answered me that the clock is a refinement resting on an already honoured toolbox. He also raised a two-part combination of B047 with a precision achievement.
responses.response: I accept that B047 is the deepest idea on the shortlist, and I still would not oppose it on merit. But the continuity objection to B010 does not persuade me, because the comb is a ruler and the lattice scheme is a different physical solution to the trap-shift problem: without the magic wavelength there is no neutral-atom clock at 1e-18. On the two-part idea, the cap of three people makes it impossible in practice: B047 with a trio plus B010 with two names is five people, and cutting either side to fit would break the credit I find most defensible on each. If a two-part prize were reached by cutting Mele, as Danielsson suggested, I would be less comfortable still. So I read the choice as one prize or the other.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B047 and rejects dropping Mele in favour of Hasan, arguing that the Z2 invariant and the graphene quantum spin Hall proposal are the conceptual origin; he also treats lattice clocks as measurement progress in an established field comparable to 2005.
responses.response: I agree with you on the narrow point that Mele belongs with Kane, and that makes the B047 attribution harder, not easier, because the experimental slot then falls to Molenkamp alone and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang stay outside. Where I disagree is the comparison with 2005. The 2005 prize honoured the comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy as methods; the lattice clock is a concrete system whose performance beat the primary standard, and I would count that as capability that did not exist before. I also take your point that the topological case is distinct from the 2016 phases prize, but you and Mehlig have both said the allocation is not settled, and that is what keeps me from moving.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B051 first but lists B010 as a safer option; in his reply to me he explained that he left the clock off his own opening ranking because the underlying ideas were recognised in 1997, 2005 and 2012, and says he would not place B051 above a clock prize.
responses.response: Thank you for stating the reason openly. I take the 1997, 2005 and 2012 list seriously, but each of those prizes honoured a different step: laser cooling, the comb, and manipulation of single ions. None addressed a scheme for holding many neutral atoms in a trap that leaves the clock transition unperturbed, and that is the specific thing the citation would name. On B051 I agree with your own caveat that the interpretation is younger than the observation, and I would add that Cao's absence from the three names is a credit problem you cannot fully solve by wording. I keep B051 as an alternative because the prediction-then-discovery chain is exactly what I trust, but on maturity and attribution B010 is ahead.

responses.point: Olsson, who moved to B010 after reading the ballots, asks whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second and whether other lattice-clock pioneers outside two names complicate the credit.
responses.response: I would not wait. The science is done and reproduced; the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows the performance and does not validate it, so tying a prize to its date would let an administrative timetable decide a scientific judgement. On other pioneers, I agree with your reading that Katori's proposal and first realisation and Ye's accuracy programme are each prize-level, and that the committee need not rank them. I would handle the others with the wording of the citation, which names the scheme and the 1e-18 outcome, not by adding names we cannot fit under the cap.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B010 and, unlike me, would not lean on the pending redefinition of the second; she also stresses framing the citation around the lattice clock, not optical clocks in general.
responses.response: I am persuaded on both points and I have changed my wording accordingly. My round-1 case said recognition was timely because the redefinition is pending; I now drop that from the argument and the citation, since it invites the objection that the committee is honouring a regulatory event. I have also tightened the citation so that it names the magic-wavelength lattice and neutral atoms explicitly, which is the boundary you proposed between the lattice clock and the ion and Al+ lines. This changes my wording, not my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig accept the magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or hold that the whole line is already honoured.

Whether the committee weighs a step change in measurement capability below a new conceptual classification of matter; I do not think this alone should decide between B010 and B047, and the chair's question shows the group is split on it.
Whether the omission of other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups is acceptable under a two-name credit; my knowledge of the priority history is from recollection and unverified here.
Whether the B047 credit can be settled in a form that Eriksson, Johansson and Mehlig accept, since that would be the strongest competing configuration.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall shared the 2005 prize, and Jun Ye is associated with that Boulder environment. I have no documented collaboration, supervisory or financial relationship with Katori or Ye, and the stay is adjacent to, not part of, the B010 credit. I raised in round 1 whether this requires recusal; no member has said it does, and I consider it a disclosure rather than a disqualification, but I will withhold my vote on B010 if the chair or committee judges otherwise. I also note a general proximity to the quantum-information candidates (B046, B041, B058) through my quantum-memory work and WACQT role; none is in my preferred configuration, and I have dropped B046 from my alternatives for that reason.
